<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par49 />verb stands in the perfect, and the narration is continued in the imperfect. Conversely, the representation of a series of future events begins with the imperfect, and is continued in the perfect. Thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=20|verse=1}}, ''In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death'' (perf.), ''and Isaiah''... ''came'' (imperf.) to ''him, and said'' (imperf.) ''to him'', &c. On the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=17}}, ''the Lord shall bring'' (imperf.) ''upon thee... days, &c.'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, ''and it shall come to pass'' (perf. {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}}) ''in that day...''

{{GHGmargin-letter|49|b}}
This progress in the sequence of time, is regularly indicated by a pregnant ''and'' (called {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}}<ref>This name best expresses the prevailing syntactical relation, for by {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} an action is always represented as the direct, or at least temporal ''consequence'' of a preceding action. Moreover, it is clear from the above examples, that the {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} can only be thus used in immediate conjunction with the verb. As soon as {{GHGterm|wāw}}, owing to an insertion (e.g. a negative), is separated from the verb, the imperfect follows instead of the perfect {{GHGterm|consecutive}}, the perfect instead of the imperfect {{GHGterm|consecutive}}. The fact that whole Books (Lev., Num., Josh., Jud., Sam., 2 Kings, Ezek., Ruth, Esth., Neh., 2 Chron.) begin with the imperfect {{GHGterm|consecutive}}, and others (Exod., 1 Kings, Ezra) with {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}, is taken as a sign of their close connexion with the historical Books now or originally preceding them. Cf., on the other hand, the independent beginning of Job and Daniel. It is a merely superficial description to call the wāw {{GHGterm|consecutive}} by the old-fashioned name {{GHGterm|wāw conversive}}, on the ground that it always converts the meaning of the respective tenses into its opposite, i.e. according to the old view, the future into the preterite, and vice versa.</ref>), which in itself is really only a variety of the ordinary {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}, but which sometimes (in the imperf.) appears with a different vocalization. Further, the tenses connected by {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} sometimes undergo a change in the tone and consequently are liable also to other variations.

{{GHGmargin-letter|49|c}}
'''2.''' The {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} of the {{GHGterm|imperfect}} is (''a'') pronounced with {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} and a {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} in the next letter, as {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקְטֹל|translate=and he killed}}; before {{GHGheb|text=א}} of the 1''st pers. sing.'' (according to {{GHGpar|22|c}}) with {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, as {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶקְטֹל|translate=and I killed}}. Exceptions are, {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲכַסֵּךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=10}} according to the ''Dikduke ha-ṭ<sup>e</sup>amim'', § 71; also {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲמֹתְתֵ֫הוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=10}} according to Qimḥi; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲגָרֵשׁ}} should be read according to Baer, and {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲ׳}} in both places in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=6}}. {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} is always omitted in the preformative {{GHGheb|text=יְ}}, in accordance with {{GHGpar|20|m}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|49|d}}
(''b'') When a shortening of the imperfect form is possible (cf. {{GHGpar|48|g}}), it takes effect, as a rule (but cf. {{GHGpar|51|n}}), after {{GHGterm|wāw consec.}}, e.g. in Hiphil {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּקְטֵל}} ({{GHGpar|53|n}}). The tendency to retract the tone from the final syllable is even stronger after {{GHGterm|wāw consec.}} than in the jussive. The throwing back of the tone on to the penultima (conditional upon its being an open syllable with a long vowel, {{GHGpar|29|a}}), further involves the greatest possible shortening of the vowel of the ultima, since the vowel then comes to stand in a toneless closed syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָקוּם}}, juss.<section end=par49 /><noinclude>
